tool.name: React
tool.tagline: Component-based JavaScript library for building user interfaces
tool.description: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components that describe what the screen should show for the current data. It powers web apps through react-dom and frameworks like Next.js and React Router, and native apps through React Native. React 19 adds Actions, the use() API, Server Components and the React Compiler.

concepts.name: What React is
concepts.summary: React is a library for building user interfaces out of components that describe what the screen should look like for given data.
concepts.why: Knowing React's core idea (UI as a function of state) makes every later API feel like a consequence rather than a rule to memorise.
concepts.body:
**React** is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Instead of writing code that finds DOM nodes and changes them step by step, you write **components**: functions that take data and return a description of the UI. When the data changes, React works out what changed and updates the real DOM for you.

This is the central idea: **UI = f(state)**. You describe what the screen should look like for the current state, not how to get there from the previous screen. That declarative style removes a whole class of bugs where the page and your variables drift out of sync.

A few things React is and isn't:

- It is a **library**, focused on rendering and state. Routing, data fetching and server rendering come from libraries or frameworks built on it (React Router, TanStack Query, Next.js, React Router's framework mode).
- It runs anywhere JavaScript does: `react-dom` targets browsers, React Native targets iOS and Android, and the same component model is used on the server.
- Modern React is written with **function components and Hooks** (`useState`, `useEffect`, ...). Class components still work but are legacy; you won't need them for new code.

React 19 adds a lot on top of the basics: **Actions** for forms and async updates, the `use()` API, **Server Components**, and the **React Compiler**, which memoizes your components automatically. This curriculum climbs from your first component to those features and to how React works inside.
takeaways: React components describe what the UI looks like for the current data
React updates the DOM for you when data changes (declarative, not imperative)
Modern React = function components + Hooks; frameworks add routing and server rendering
pitfalls: Thinking of React as a full framework: routing and data fetching come from other libraries or a framework.

quiz.q: What does 'declarative' mean in the context of React?
options: You describe the UI for the current state and React makes the DOM match
You call DOM methods in the right order to update the page
You declare all variables with const
You write HTML templates in separate files
quiz.explain: React components return a description of the desired UI; React figures out the DOM operations needed to get there.

concepts.name: Creating a project with Vite
concepts.summary: Scaffold a React app with Vite, understand its files, and run the dev server with fast refresh.
concepts.why: Every React project starts with a build setup; Vite is the standard lightweight choice when you aren't using a framework.
concepts.body:
React code uses JSX and ES modules, so it needs a build tool. For a client-side app the usual choice is **Vite**: a fast dev server plus a production bundler. (Create React App is deprecated; if you need routing, data loading and server rendering from day one, the React docs recommend a framework such as Next.js or React Router instead.)

Create and run a project:

```bash
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```

Use `--template react` for plain JavaScript. The dev server (usually on port 5173) supports **Fast Refresh**: edit a component and it updates in the browser while keeping its state.

The important files:

- `index.html` is the real entry point; it contains `<div id="root">` and loads `src/main.tsx`.
- `src/main.tsx` creates a React root on that div and renders `<App />` inside `<StrictMode>`.
- `src/App.tsx` is your first component. Everything else is components imported from here.
- `vite.config.ts` registers `@vitejs/plugin-react`, which handles JSX and Fast Refresh.

`npm run build` produces static files in `dist/` that any web server can host, and `npm run preview` serves that build locally. The imports at the top of each file are ordinary ES modules: `import { useState } from "react"` pulls a named export from the `react` package.
takeaways: `npm create vite@latest app -- --template react` (or `react-ts`) scaffolds a project
`createRoot(el).render(<App />)` from `react-dom/client` mounts React into the page
`npm run dev` for development, `npm run build` for static production files
pitfalls: Starting new projects with Create React App, which is deprecated and unmaintained.

quiz.q: In a Vite React app, what does createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />) do?
options: Compiles JSX to JavaScript
Starts the development server
Takes over the #root DOM element and renders the App component tree into it
Creates a new HTML file for the app
quiz.explain: createRoot attaches React to an existing DOM node; render puts the component tree inside it.

concepts.name: Your first components
concepts.summary: Define components as capitalised functions that return JSX, nest them, and export them from modules.
concepts.why: Components are the unit of everything in React; splitting UI into small components is the main design skill.
concepts.body:
A **component** is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns markup (JSX). You use it like an HTML tag: ```jsx function Avatar() { return ; } ``` Then `` anywhere renders that image. Components can render other components, so an app is a **tree**: `App` renders `Header`, `Feed` and `Sidebar`, `Feed` renders many `Post`s, and so on. The rules: - **Capitalise names.** `` is treated as an HTML tag; `` calls your function. - **Return one root.** Wrap siblings in a `
` or a **Fragment** `<>...`, which adds no DOM node. - **Define components at the top level** of a module, never inside another component. A component defined inside another is a new function on every render, so React throws away its state and DOM each time. - **Export them** to use them from other files: `export default function Profile()` or a named `export function Avatar()`. Keep components small and focused. A good rule of thumb: if a piece of UI is reused, or a component's JSX no longer fits on a screen, extract a component. Component boundaries also become state and performance boundaries later, so they are worth getting right.
takeaways: A component is a capitalised function that returns JSX
Use `<>...</>` (Fragment) to return several elements without an extra DOM node
Declare components at module top level and import/export them like any module
pitfalls: Defining a component inside another component, which resets its state on every render.

quiz.q: Why should you not declare function Item() inside the body of function List()?
options: It is a syntax error
Item can then only be used once
JSX cannot reference inner functions
Item becomes a new component type every render, so its state and DOM are recreated
quiz.explain: React compares component types by identity; a freshly created function each render looks like a different component.

concepts.name: JSX
concepts.summary: Write markup in JavaScript with JSX: curly braces for expressions, camelCase attributes, className and style objects.
concepts.why: JSX is how every component describes its output; its few rules differ from HTML in ways that trip up beginners.
concepts.body:
**JSX** is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. The build tool compiles each tag to a function call (`jsx("h1", {...})`) that creates a plain object describing the element. So JSX is just JavaScript values: you can store it in variables, return it, and pass it around. Curly braces switch back to JavaScript. Inside `{}` you can put any **expression**: a variable, `user.name`, `formatDate(d)`, a ternary. Statements like `if` or `for` don't fit inside braces; compute values before the `return` instead. How JSX differs from HTML: - Every tag must be closed: ``, `
`. - Attributes are camelCase JavaScript property names: `className` (not `class`), `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`. `aria-*` and `data-*` keep their dashes. - `style` takes an object: `style={{ color: "red", fontSize: 14 }}`. The outer braces mean "JavaScript", the inner ones are the object. - Text in braces is escaped automatically, so `{userInput}` can't inject HTML. That's a security feature. What renders: strings and numbers appear as text; `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render nothing; arrays render each item. Objects are not valid children, so `{user}` throws; render `{user.name}`. Comments inside JSX go in braces: `{/* note */}`.
takeaways: `{}` embeds any JavaScript expression; compute statements before `return`
Use `className`, `htmlFor` and camelCase event/attribute names; close every tag
`style={{ ... }}` takes an object; text in braces is auto-escaped
pitfalls: Rendering an object directly (`{user}`) instead of one of its fields; React throws 'Objects are not valid as a React child'.

quiz.q: Which JSX is valid?
options: {if (ok) 'yes'}
{ok ? 'yes' : 'no'}
yes
quiz.explain: Braces take expressions (a ternary works, if doesn't), style needs an object, and every tag must be closed.

concepts.name: Props
concepts.summary: Pass data to components through props, destructure them, set defaults, and pass JSX as children.
concepts.why: Props are how components are configured and composed; nearly every component you write takes some.
concepts.body:
**Props** are the inputs to a component. You pass them like HTML attributes, and React collects them into one object that is the function's first argument:

```jsx
<Avatar person={{ name: "Lin" }} size={100} />

function Avatar({ person, size = 48 }) { ... }
```

Destructuring in the parameter list is the idiomatic style, and a default value (`size = 48`) applies when the prop is missing or `undefined`. Any JavaScript value can be a prop: strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions and JSX.

The special **`children`** prop holds whatever you nest between a component's tags. It is how you build wrappers like cards, layouts and dialogs that don't need to know what's inside them:

```jsx
<Card><Avatar person={p} /></Card>   // Card receives children
```

You can forward a bag of props with spread, `<Avatar {...props} />`, which is handy in thin wrappers; use it sparingly, as it hides what is being passed.

Props are **read-only**. A component must never modify its props; they belong to the parent. When something needs to change over time, that's **state**, which you'll meet shortly. When the parent re-renders with new props, the child simply renders again with the new values.

In TypeScript, describe props with a type: `function Avatar({ size }: { size: number })`, or a named `type AvatarProps = {...}`.
takeaways: Props arrive as one object; destructure them and give defaults in the parameter list
`children` is whatever is nested between the tags, enabling wrapper components
Props are read-only; values that change over time belong in state
pitfalls: Mutating a prop (e.g. `props.items.push(x)`): the parent owns that data and won't know it changed.

quiz.q: Given function Badge({ label = 'New' }), what label does <Badge label={undefined} /> show?
options: Nothing
'undefined'
'New'
It throws an error
quiz.explain: Destructuring defaults apply when the value is undefined, whether the prop is missing or passed as undefined.

quiz.q: What does a Layout component receive in children for <Layout><Nav /><Main /></Layout>?
options: The two elements <Nav /> and <Main />
Nothing; children must be passed explicitly as a prop
Only the first element
The rendered DOM nodes
quiz.explain: Nested JSX is passed in the children prop; here it is the two elements.

concepts.name: Conditional rendering
concepts.summary: Show different UI depending on conditions with if/return, the ternary operator and &&.
concepts.why: Almost every component has states like loading, empty or error that render differently.
concepts.body:
Because JSX is JavaScript, conditional UI uses ordinary JavaScript. There are three common patterns.

**Early return with `if`** when a whole branch differs:

```jsx
if (!user) return <LoginPrompt />;
return <Dashboard user={user} />;
```

Returning `null` renders nothing, which is how a component hides itself.

**The ternary** `cond ? a : b` inside JSX for small either/or choices: `{isPacked ? <s>{name}</s> : name}`.

**Logical AND** `cond && <Thing />` when there is no else branch. If the condition is false, React renders nothing.

The classic gotcha with `&&`: if the left side is the number `0`, the expression evaluates to `0`, and React renders a literal 0. `{messages.length && <Badge />}` shows "0" when the list is empty. Make the left side a real boolean: `{messages.length > 0 && <Badge />}`.

You can also put JSX in a variable and assign it conditionally before the `return`, which keeps complicated logic out of the markup:

```jsx
let content = <Spinner />;
if (error) content = <ErrorMessage error={error} />;
else if (data) content = <Results data={data} />;
```

When the nested ternaries start to pile up, that variable pattern, or extracting a small component, is the readable fix.
takeaways: Use `if` with early return for whole branches; return `null` to render nothing
Use `cond ? a : b` for either/or and `cond && x` for show/hide
Keep the left side of `&&` boolean: `count > 0 && ...`, not `count && ...`
pitfalls: `{items.length && <List />}` renders a stray 0 when the array is empty.

quiz.q:
What does {count &&

Items

} render when count is 0?
options: Nothing
The text 0
Items
false
quiz.explain: 0 && x evaluates to 0, and numbers are rendered as text; false, null and undefined render nothing.

concepts.name: Rendering lists and keys
concepts.summary: Turn arrays into elements with map and filter, and give each item a stable key so React can track it.
concepts.why: Lists are everywhere, and wrong keys cause subtle bugs where state sticks to the wrong row.
concepts.body:
To render a list, transform your data array into an array of JSX elements, usually with `map`, and filter first with `filter` if needed: ```jsx const items = people .filter(p => p.active) .map(p =>
  • {p.name}
    • ); return
      {items}
    ; ``` Every element in an array needs a **`key`** prop: a string or number that uniquely identifies that item among its siblings. Keys tell React which item is which between renders. When you insert, delete or reorder items, React uses keys to move the existing DOM nodes and component state along with the right data instead of rebuilding everything or, worse, pairing state with the wrong item. Good keys come from the data: database ids, slugs, or ids you generate once when the item is created (`crypto.randomUUID()`). Rules: - Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally. - Keys must be **stable**: the same item gets the same key on every render. - Don't use the array index if the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted; the index then refers to a different item and any state (like a typed-in input) follows the position, not the item. Index is acceptable only for static lists. - Never generate keys during render (`key={Math.random()}`); every render then creates brand-new components. The key goes on the outermost element returned from `map`. If you need to return several elements per item, use `` (import `Fragment` from `react`), since the short `<>` syntax can't take a key. Keys are not passed to your component as a prop; pass the id separately if the child needs it.
takeaways: Render arrays with `map` (and `filter`); each element needs a `key`
Keys must be unique among siblings and stable across renders, ideally ids from the data
Avoid index keys for lists that change order or contents; never use random keys
pitfalls: Using the array index as key in an editable or sortable list, so input state ends up on the wrong row.

quiz.q: A todo list uses key={index}. You delete the first todo; each row has an uncontrolled text input. What happens?
options: Everything works correctly
React throws a duplicate key error
All inputs are cleared
The typed text stays in place by position, so it now appears next to the wrong todo
quiz.explain: With index keys, item 2 now has key 0, so React reuses the first row's DOM and state for it.

concepts.name: Responding to events
concepts.summary: Attach event handlers with onClick and friends, pass handlers as props, and use the event object.
concepts.why: Events are how users interact with your UI and the trigger for nearly every state change.
concepts.body:
You handle events by passing a **function** to a camelCase prop such as `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit` or `onKeyDown`:

```jsx
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
```

Pass the function, don't call it. `onClick={handleClick()}` runs during render and passes its return value. When you need arguments, wrap it: `onClick={() => deleteItem(id)}`.

Handlers receive a **synthetic event** that wraps the native one with the same interface across browsers: `e.target`, `e.preventDefault()`, `e.stopPropagation()`, `e.key`. Events bubble up through the React tree just like in the DOM, so a click on a button also reaches an `onClick` on its parent unless you stop propagation. (React attaches its listeners at the root, not on each element.)

A very common pattern is passing handlers **as props**. The parent decides what happens; the child decides when:

```jsx
function Toolbar({ onPlay }) {
  return <button onClick={onPlay}>Play</button>;
}
```

By convention, props that take handlers are named `onSomething` and the functions that implement them `handleSomething`.

For forms, call `e.preventDefault()` in an `onSubmit` handler to stop the browser's full-page submit, or use React 19's `action` prop, covered later. Handlers are where side effects belong: they may update state, call APIs and log analytics, because they run in response to a user action rather than during rendering.
takeaways: Pass a function to `onClick`, don't call it: `onClick={fn}` or `onClick={() => fn(id)}`
Events bubble through the React tree; `e.stopPropagation()` and `e.preventDefault()` work as in the DOM
Name handler props `onX` and implementations `handleX`; side effects belong in handlers
pitfalls: Writing `onClick={remove(id)}`, which calls `remove` on every render instead of on click.

quiz.q: What is wrong with <button onClick={setOpen(true)}>Open</button>?
options: setOpen(true) runs during rendering instead of on click, which causes an infinite re-render loop
Nothing
Event handlers cannot call state setters
onClick must be lowercase
quiz.explain: The expression is evaluated during render; use onClick={() => setOpen(true)} to defer it to the click.

concepts.name: State with useState
concepts.summary: Give a component memory with useState, understand that state is a snapshot, and use updater functions.
concepts.why: State is what makes a UI interactive; misunderstanding when it updates is the most common React bug.
concepts.body:
Regular variables don't survive re-renders, and changing them doesn't tell React to update. For data that changes over time, use **state**:

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

`useState` returns the current value and a setter. Calling the setter stores the new value and **schedules a re-render**; on that render `useState` returns the new value. Each component instance has its own state: render `<Counter />` twice and you get two independent counts.

`useState` is a **Hook**. Hooks are functions starting with `use`, and they must be called at the top level of a component (not inside conditions, loops or nested functions), because React matches them up by call order.

The key mental model: **state is a snapshot**. During one render, `count` is a constant. Setting it doesn't change the variable you already have, it requests a new render:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);   // still count + 1: both read the same snapshot
console.log(count);    // old value
```

React also **batches** updates from the same event into one re-render. When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an **updater function**, which React applies to the latest queued state:

```jsx
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);  // +2
```

If initial state is expensive to compute, pass a function: `useState(() => buildIndex(data))` runs only on the first render.

Only store what can't be computed. If a value can be derived from props or other state (a full name from first and last, a filtered list), compute it during render instead of keeping it in sync in state.
takeaways: `const [v, setV] = useState(init)`; calling the setter schedules a re-render
State is a snapshot: the variable doesn't change until the next render
Use `setV(prev => next)` when the new value depends on the old one
Call Hooks only at the top level; derive values instead of duplicating them in state
pitfalls: Reading state right after setting it and expecting the new value.
Copying props into state and then wondering why it doesn't update when the prop changes.

quiz.q: count is 0. A click handler runs setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); setCount(c => c + 1). What is count after the re-render?
quiz.explain: The first two both set 0 + 1 = 1 from the snapshot; the updater then adds 1 to the queued value, giving 2.

quiz.q: Why must Hooks not be called inside an if statement?
options: It is slower
Hooks can only be called in event handlers
TypeScript cannot type them
React identifies each Hook by its call order, which must be the same on every render
quiz.explain: State is stored in a list per component and matched by position, so the order of Hook calls must never change.

concepts.name: Updating objects and arrays
concepts.summary: Treat objects and arrays in state as immutable: copy them with spread, map and filter instead of mutating.
concepts.why: Mutating state is the classic cause of 'my UI doesn't update'; immutable updates are the fix and a core React habit.
concepts.body:
State can hold objects and arrays, but you must treat them as **immutable**. React decides whether to re-render by comparing the old and new value with `Object.is`. If you mutate the existing object and pass the same reference back, React sees no change, and even if something else triggers a render, you've corrupted the previous snapshot.

So instead of changing data, **create a new copy** with the change applied.

Objects: spread the old fields, then override.

```jsx
setPerson({ ...person, email: newEmail });
setPerson({ ...person, address: { ...person.address, city } }); // nested: copy each level
```

Arrays: use methods that return a new array.

- Add: `[...items, item]` or `[item, ...items]`
- Remove: `items.filter(i => i.id !== id)`
- Replace or update one: `items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i)`
- Insert: `[...items.slice(0, n), item, ...items.slice(n)]`
- Sort/reverse: copy first, `[...items].sort(cmp)`, or use `toSorted()` / `toReversed()`

Avoid `push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and direct assignment (`items[0] = x`, `person.name = x`) on state.

If deeply nested updates get painful, that's often a sign the state should be **flattened** (store items by id, keep `selectedId` rather than a copy of the selected object). The **Immer** library (`useImmer`) lets you write mutating-looking code that produces immutable copies, which some teams prefer for complex structures.
takeaways: Never mutate state; build a new object or array and pass it to the setter
Objects: `{ ...obj, field: v }`; nested objects need a copy at each level
Arrays: add with spread, remove with `filter`, update with `map`, sort a copy
pitfalls: `items.push(x); setItems(items)` passes the same array reference, so React may skip the update.

quiz.q: Which update correctly marks the todo with id 7 as done?
options: todos.find(t => t.id === 7).done = true; setTodos(todos)
setTodos(todos.map(t => t.id === 7 ? { ...t, done: true } : t))
setTodos(todos.map(t => { if (t.id === 7) t.done = true; return t; }))
todos[6].done = true; setTodos([...todos])
quiz.explain: Only the map with a spread copy creates a new object for the changed item; the others mutate existing state objects.

concepts.name: Forms and controlled inputs
concepts.summary: Build forms with controlled inputs bound to state, or uncontrolled inputs read on submit with FormData.
concepts.why: Forms are where most user input enters an app, and the controlled/uncontrolled distinction shapes how you handle it.
takeaways: Controlled: `value` + `onChange` bound to state; React state is the source of truth
Uncontrolled: `defaultValue` and read values on submit with `new FormData(form)`
Call `e.preventDefault()` in `onSubmit` (or use the React 19 `action` prop)
pitfalls: Initialising controlled-input state to `undefined`, which flips the input from uncontrolled to controlled.

quiz.q: An <input value={text} /> has no onChange handler. What happens when the user types?
options: The text updates normally
React throws an error and unmounts the form
The input does not change, because its value is always forced to the state value
The input becomes uncontrolled automatically
quiz.explain: A controlled input shows exactly the value prop; without an onChange that updates state, typing has no effect (and React warns).

concepts.name: Thinking in React and lifting state
concepts.summary: Break a UI into components, find the minimal state, decide which component owns it, and lift state up to share it.
concepts.why: Deciding where state lives is the core design decision in every React app; get it right and the rest follows.
concepts.body:
The React docs describe a design process that scales from a widget to an app:

- **Break the UI into a component hierarchy.** Draw boxes around parts of the mockup; each box with one responsibility is a component.
- **Build a static version** that renders from props, with no state.
- **Find the minimal state.** Ask of each piece of data: is it passed in from a parent? Does it stay the same over time? Can it be computed from other state or props? If any answer is yes, it's not state. In a filterable product table, the product list (a prop) and the filtered list (derived) aren't state; the search text and the "in stock only" checkbox are.
- **Decide who owns each piece of state**: the closest common parent of all components that use it.
- **Add inverse data flow**: children change the owner's state by calling callbacks passed down as props.

When two siblings need the same data, **lift the state up**: remove it from the children, put it in their parent, and pass the value and a setter-like callback down. The children become **controlled** components, driven by props, which makes them easy to coordinate (only one accordion panel open at a time, say).

Data flows **down** through props and events flow **up** through callbacks. That one-way flow is why React apps stay debuggable: for any value on screen, there's exactly one component that owns it.

Avoid duplicating state (storing `selectedItem` as a copy when `selectedId` would do) and avoid contradictory state (`isSending` and `isSent` both true). If state lives too high, many components re-render needlessly and props get passed through many layers; context and composition help with that later.
takeaways: State is data that changes, isn't passed in, and can't be computed from anything else
Put state in the closest common parent of the components that use it
Data flows down as props; changes flow up through callback props
pitfalls: Keeping the same data in two components' state and trying to sync them instead of lifting it up.

quiz.q: A SearchBar and a ProductTable (siblings) both need the search text. Where should that state live?
options: In their closest common parent, passed down as props
In SearchBar, passed to ProductTable with a ref
In both components, kept in sync with an effect
In a global variable
quiz.explain: Lift shared state to the nearest common parent; it passes the value to both and a setter callback to SearchBar.

quiz.q: Which of these should NOT be state in a filterable list?
options: The text in the search box
The list of items filtered by the search text
Whether the 'show archived' checkbox is ticked
Which item the user has selected
quiz.explain: The filtered list can be computed during render from the items and the search text, so it shouldn't be stored.

concepts.name: Pure components and Strict Mode
concepts.summary: Keep rendering pure (same inputs, same JSX, no side effects) and use Strict Mode to catch impurity during development.
concepts.why: React relies on purity to re-render, pause and reuse work safely; impure components break in subtle, intermittent ways.
concepts.body:
React assumes every component is a **pure function** during rendering:

- **Same inputs, same output.** Given the same props, state and context, it returns the same JSX.
- **No side effects while rendering.** It doesn't change variables or objects that existed before the render, doesn't touch the DOM, doesn't start requests or timers, doesn't write to `localStorage`.

Creating and mutating *local* variables is fine; it's changing pre-existing things that's forbidden. A counter defined outside the component and incremented during render, for example, gives different results each time the component renders.

Why this matters: React may call your component more often than you expect, render it and throw the result away (concurrent rendering), render parts of the tree in a different order, or skip rendering entirely when it can reuse a previous result (the React Compiler relies on this). Pure components make all of that invisible.

Side effects still have a home:

- **Event handlers** for effects caused by a user action (click, submit, type).
- **Effects** (`useEffect`) for synchronizing with something outside React because the component is on screen.

**Strict Mode** (`<StrictMode>` wrapping your app, as Vite's template does) helps find impurity in development only. It renders each component twice, runs effects' setup, cleanup and setup again on mount, and does the same for ref callbacks. Pure code behaves identically; impure code shows doubled output or broken behaviour, pointing you at the bug. That's why you might see console logs twice in development. Production builds don't double anything.
takeaways: Rendering must be pure: same inputs, same JSX, no changes to pre-existing values
Put side effects in event handlers, or in effects when they sync with an external system
Strict Mode double-renders and re-runs effects in development to expose impure code
pitfalls: Removing `<StrictMode>` to 'fix' double logs or a double request instead of fixing the impure code or adding effect cleanup.

quiz.q: Under Strict Mode in development, a component logs once per render. You see two logs on mount. Why?
options: The component has a bug that renders it twice in production too
React always renders every component twice
The log is duplicated by the browser console
Strict Mode intentionally renders components twice in development to detect impure rendering
quiz.explain: Strict Mode double-invokes rendering in development only; pure components are unaffected by it.

concepts.name: useEffect and synchronizing
concepts.summary: Use effects to synchronize a component with external systems, with correct dependencies and cleanup, and know when not to use one.
concepts.why: Effects are the most misused Hook; knowing what they are for prevents bugs, wasted renders and race conditions.
takeaways: Effects synchronize with external systems and run after the commit
List every reactive value the effect reads in its dependencies; return a cleanup that undoes setup
Derived data belongs in render, user-triggered work in event handlers, not in effects
pitfalls: Omitting dependencies to stop an effect re-running, which leaves it reading stale values.
Chains of effects that set state to trigger other effects instead of computing values during render.

quiz.q: store.subscribe(cb) returns an unsubscribe function. Does useEffect(() => store.subscribe(cb), [cb]) clean up correctly?
options: Yes: the arrow function returns the unsubscribe function, which React uses as the cleanup
No: the cleanup must be written as return () => { ... } in a block body
No: subscriptions can only be cleaned up when the dependency array is empty
No: cleanup only runs in production builds
quiz.explain: The concise arrow body returns subscribe's return value (an unsubscribe function), which React uses as the cleanup.

quiz.q: A component stores fullName in state and updates it in an effect whenever firstName or lastName changes. What's the better approach?
options: Add fullName to the effect's dependencies
Use useLayoutEffect so it updates sooner
Compute const fullName = firstName + ' ' + lastName during render
Move the effect to the parent component
quiz.explain: Derived values should be calculated during rendering; the effect causes an extra render with a stale value.

concepts.name: Refs, DOM access and portals
concepts.summary: Keep mutable values that don't trigger renders with useRef, reach DOM nodes through ref, and render elsewhere with createPortal.
concepts.why: Focusing inputs, measuring elements, holding timer ids and integrating non-React code all need refs.
takeaways: `useRef` holds a mutable `.current` that persists across renders without triggering them
Pass a ref to `ref={...}` to get the DOM node; in React 19 `ref` is a normal prop for components
Don't read/write refs during render; use `createPortal` to render into another DOM node
pitfalls: Storing something in a ref that the UI displays, so the screen doesn't update when it changes.

quiz.q: You store a click count in a ref and render {countRef.current}. Clicking increments countRef.current. What does the user see?
options: The count updating on every click
The count updating once per second
An error, because refs can't be rendered
The old value, until something else causes a re-render
quiz.explain: Changing ref.current doesn't trigger a render; values that are displayed belong in state.

quiz.q: What stays the same for content rendered with createPortal into document.body?
options: Its position in the DOM tree
Its position in the React tree, so context and event bubbling follow the React parent
Its CSS inheritance from the parent element
Nothing; it becomes a separate React root
quiz.explain: Portals change only where the DOM nodes go; React-wise the children remain under their parent.

concepts.name: Custom Hooks
concepts.summary: Extract reusable stateful logic into your own use-prefixed functions that call other Hooks.
concepts.why: Custom Hooks are React's main tool for reusing behaviour and keeping components readable.
takeaways: A custom Hook is a `use`-prefixed function that calls other Hooks
It shares logic, not state: every call has its own state
Name Hooks by purpose (`useOnlineStatus`), not by lifecycle (`useMount`)
pitfalls: Prefixing a plain helper with `use` even though it calls no Hooks, which needlessly restricts where it can be called.

quiz.q: Two components both call useCounter(). One increments its count. What happens to the other's count?
options: It increments too, because they share the Hook
It resets to the initial value
Nothing; each call has its own independent state
React throws because a Hook was used twice
quiz.explain: Custom Hooks reuse stateful logic, but each call creates separate state for the calling component.

concepts.name: Context
concepts.summary: Pass data deeply without prop drilling using createContext, a provider, and useContext or use.
concepts.why: Themes, the current user, locale and similar app-wide values need to reach distant components cleanly.
concepts.body:
Passing props through many layers that don't use them (**prop drilling**) gets tedious. **Context** lets a parent make a value available to every component below it, however deep.

Three steps:

```jsx
const ThemeContext = createContext("light");          // 1. create, with a default
<ThemeContext value="dark"><Page /></ThemeContext>     // 2. provide
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);                // 3. read
```

In React 19 you render the context itself as the provider (`<ThemeContext value=...>`); `<ThemeContext.Provider>` still works but is on its way out. A component reads the value from the **nearest** provider above it; with none, it gets the default from `createContext`. Providers can be nested to override values for a subtree.

React 19's `use(ThemeContext)` reads context too, and unlike `useContext` it can be called inside conditions and loops.

When the provided value changes, every component reading that context re-renders. Two consequences:

- If you provide an object, `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object each render, re-rendering all consumers. Memoize it with `useMemo` (or let the React Compiler do it), or split it into separate contexts for rarely and frequently changing parts.
- Context isn't a substitute for a state manager with fine-grained subscriptions; for large, fast-changing shared state consider an external store.

A very common pattern is context **plus a reducer**: keep state in a top-level component with `useReducer` and provide both state and `dispatch` via context, wrapped in a custom Hook like `useTasks()`.

Before reaching for context, try composition: passing JSX as `children` often removes the drilling with no new concepts.
takeaways: `createContext(default)`, provide with `<Ctx value={...}>`, read with `useContext(Ctx)` or `use(Ctx)`
Consumers read the nearest provider above them and re-render when its value changes
Keep provided objects stable and split contexts by update frequency
pitfalls: Calling `useContext` in the same component that renders the provider: it reads the provider above, not its own.

quiz.q: A component calls useContext(ThemeContext) but no ThemeContext provider exists above it. What does it get?
options: The default value passed to createContext
undefined, always
An error is thrown
The value from the most recently rendered provider anywhere
quiz.explain: Without a provider in the ancestors, the context's default value is used.

concepts.name: Reducers with useReducer
concepts.summary: Consolidate complex state updates into a reducer function that handles dispatched actions.
concepts.why: When many event handlers update related state, a reducer makes the logic testable and easier to follow.
takeaways: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial)`; handlers dispatch actions
Reducers are pure: `(state, action) => newState`, never mutating
Prefer a reducer when related state changes together or logic needs testing
pitfalls: Doing side effects (fetching, saving) inside the reducer instead of in the event handler.

quiz.q: Where should an API call that saves the cart go when using useReducer?
options: Inside the reducer's case for 'saved'
In the event handler (or an Action), with dispatch used to record the result
In the initial state
In the default case of the switch
quiz.explain: Reducers must be pure; side effects belong in handlers, which then dispatch actions describing what happened.

concepts.name: Data fetching patterns
concepts.summary: Fetch data in effects without race conditions, and know when to use a data library, a framework loader or use() instead.
concepts.why: Every real app loads data; naive fetching causes race conditions, waterfalls and duplicated loading logic.
takeaways: Fetch in an effect keyed by its inputs, with an ignore flag or AbortController against races
Real apps use a data library (TanStack Query, SWR) or framework loaders for caching and no waterfalls
With React 19, `use(promise)` + Suspense reads cached or passed-in promises during render
pitfalls: Forgetting cleanup, so a slow earlier response overwrites the data for the current id.
Creating a new promise during render and passing it to `use()`, causing endless suspending.

quiz.q: A profile page fetches in useEffect keyed by userId with no cleanup. The user clicks A then quickly B; A's response arrives last. What's shown?
options: B's profile
A loading spinner forever
An error
A's profile, even though B is selected
quiz.explain: Without an ignore flag or abort, the late response for A calls setState after B's and wins the race.

concepts.name: Styling approaches
concepts.summary: Choose between plain CSS, CSS Modules, utility CSS like Tailwind and CSS-in-JS, and use className and style correctly.
concepts.why: Every project picks a styling strategy early; knowing the trade-offs avoids painful migrations.
concepts.body:
React doesn't prescribe styling; it just gives you `className` and `style`. The main approaches:

- **Plain CSS files** imported into a module (`import "./App.css"`). Vite bundles them. Simple, but class names are global, so collisions grow with the app.
- **CSS Modules**: name the file `Button.module.css`, then `import styles from "./Button.module.css"` and use `className={styles.primary}`. Class names are scoped to the file automatically. Zero runtime cost, supported by Vite and all frameworks out of the box.
- **Utility-first CSS** such as **Tailwind**: compose small classes in JSX (`className="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-600"`). Very popular with React because styles live next to markup and unused CSS is stripped.
- **CSS-in-JS** (styled-components, Emotion) defines styles in JavaScript. Runtime-based libraries add cost and don't fit well with Server Components; zero-runtime options (vanilla-extract, Panda, StyleX) compile to static CSS.

Whatever you choose, conditional classes are just strings. Build them with a template literal or a helper like `clsx`: `className={clsx("tab", isActive && "tab-active")}`.

The `style` prop takes an object with camelCase properties and is best for truly dynamic values (a computed width, a CSS variable): `style={{ "--progress": pct + "%" }}`. Prefer classes for everything static.

React 19 adds built-in support for `<link rel="stylesheet" precedence="default">` anywhere in the tree: React hoists it to the head, de-duplicates it and waits for it to load before revealing the content that needs it. It also hoists `<title>` and `<meta>` rendered inside components into the document head.
takeaways: `className` takes a string; build conditional classes with `clsx` or a helper
CSS Modules scope class names per file; Tailwind keeps utility classes in JSX
Use `style` for dynamic values; React 19 hoists `<title>`, `<meta>` and stylesheets
pitfalls: Choosing a runtime CSS-in-JS library for a Server Components app, where it requires client-only workarounds.

quiz.q: What does importing styles from './Card.module.css' give you that importing './Card.css' does not?
options: Class names that are locally scoped to the component, avoiding global collisions
Faster CSS parsing in the browser
Inline styles on every element
Automatic dark mode
quiz.explain: CSS Modules rewrite class names to unique ones and expose them as an object, so they can't clash.

concepts.name: Routing with React Router
concepts.summary: Map URLs to components with React Router: routes, nested layouts, links, URL params and navigation.
concepts.why: Any multi-page app needs URLs that reflect what's on screen; React itself doesn't include a router.
concepts.body:
React has no built-in router; the most widely used is **React Router** (v7, imported from `react-router`). It can run as a plain library in a Vite app or as a full framework with loaders and SSR. The library usage looks like this:

```jsx
<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
      <Route index element={<Home />} />
      <Route path="users/:userId" element={<User />} />
      <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
    </Route>
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>
```

Key ideas:

- **Routes match the URL** and render their `element`. Paths can contain **dynamic segments** (`:userId`), read with `useParams()`.
- **Nested routes** build layouts. A parent route renders shared UI (header, sidebar) and an `<Outlet />` where the matching child appears. `index` marks the child shown at the parent's own path.
- **Navigate without reloading** using `<Link to="/users/42">` or `<NavLink>` (which knows when it's active). Plain `<a href>` triggers a full page load.
- **Programmatic navigation** after an action: `const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/done")`.
- **Query strings** via `useSearchParams()`, which is a good home for filter and sort state because it survives reloads and can be shared as a link.

React Router's data mode (`createBrowserRouter` with `loader` and `action` per route) and framework mode go further: data loads in parallel with code before rendering, avoiding effect waterfalls. Next.js and TanStack Router are popular alternatives with file-based or type-safe routing.

On a static host, configure the server to serve `index.html` for unknown paths, or direct links to `/users/42` will 404.
takeaways: Routes map URL patterns to elements; `:param` segments are read with `useParams`
Nested routes plus `<Outlet />` give shared layouts
Use `<Link>`/`useNavigate` for client-side navigation; keep shareable UI state in the URL
pitfalls: Using `<a href>` for internal links, which reloads the whole app and loses state.

quiz.q: In a nested route setup, where does the matching child route render?
options: Replacing the parent's element entirely
At the end of document.body
Wherever the parent renders <Outlet />
In a new browser tab
quiz.explain: The parent route's element renders shared layout and an <Outlet /> placeholder for the active child.

concepts.name: Testing components
concepts.summary: Test components the way users use them with Vitest and React Testing Library: render, query by role, interact, assert.
concepts.why: Tests that exercise behaviour rather than implementation let you refactor and upgrade React with confidence.
takeaways: Render, query by role/label, interact with user-event, assert on what the user sees
`getBy` throws, `queryBy` returns null, `findBy` waits for async UI
Mock the network (MSW), not your components' internals
pitfalls: Using `getBy...` right after triggering an async load; use `await findBy...` so the test waits.

quiz.q: Which query should you use to wait for a heading that appears after data loads?
options: screen.getByRole('heading')
screen.queryByRole('heading')
container.querySelector('h1')
await screen.findByRole('heading')
quiz.explain: findBy queries return a promise that retries until the element appears or a timeout passes.

concepts.name: Rendering and reconciliation
concepts.summary: Understand trigger, render and commit, how React diffs trees by type and key, and when state is preserved or reset.
concepts.why: Knowing exactly when components re-render and when state survives explains most performance issues and 'my state reset' bugs.
concepts.body:
Every screen update goes through three steps:

- **Trigger**: the initial `root.render()`, or a state update in some component.
- **Render**: React calls your components to compute the new JSX. When a component re-renders, by default **all its descendants re-render too**, whether or not their props changed.
- **Commit**: React applies the minimal set of DOM changes. If the output is the same, the DOM isn't touched; rendering is not the same as repainting.

Producing the new tree and comparing it with the previous one is **reconciliation**. React doesn't do a general tree diff (that would be O(n³)); it uses two heuristics:

- Elements of **different types** at the same position produce different subtrees. Switching `<div>` to `<section>`, or `<Counter>` to `<Timer>`, unmounts the old subtree (losing its state and DOM) and mounts a new one.
- Among children, **keys** identify which element is which across renders.

This defines when **state is preserved**: state belongs to a position in the tree, not to the component function. Same component type at the same position keeps its state, even if you pass different props. `{isAdmin ? <Profile user={a} /> : <Profile user={b} />}` keeps one `Profile`'s state for both users.

To **reset** state deliberately, change the key: `<Profile key={user.id} user={user} />` makes each user a different component instance. That's the idiomatic way to reset a form when the selected item changes, instead of an effect.

Corollaries: never define components inside other components (new type every render), and don't flip a subtree's wrapper element type unless you want a remount. Because re-rendering cascades, pushing state down to the component that needs it, or passing static JSX as `children`, keeps renders small even before any memoization.
takeaways: Updates go trigger, render, commit; re-rendering a parent re-renders its children by default
Same type at the same position preserves state; a different type or key remounts
Change a component's `key` to reset its state on purpose
pitfalls: Wrapping content in a different element conditionally (`<div>` vs `<span>`) and unexpectedly losing child state.

quiz.q: {edit ? <Form initial={a} /> : <Form initial={b} />} - the user types into the form, then edit flips. What happens to the typed text?
options: It's cleared because the props changed
It's preserved because the same component type is at the same position
React throws a reconciliation error
It moves to a new DOM node
quiz.explain: React sees a Form at the same position both times and keeps its state; add distinct keys to reset it.

quiz.q: When a parent component re-renders, what happens to a child whose props did not change (no memo)?
options: It is skipped automatically
It is unmounted and remounted
It re-renders too
Only its effects re-run
quiz.explain: By default React re-renders the whole subtree; memo or the React Compiler is needed to skip unchanged children.

concepts.name: Memoization and the React Compiler
concepts.summary: Skip unnecessary work with memo, useMemo and useCallback, and let the React Compiler apply memoization automatically.
concepts.why: Memoization fixes real slowdowns, but misapplied it adds complexity; the Compiler changes when you need it by hand.
concepts.body:
Because re-rendering cascades, you sometimes want to skip work. React offers three tools:

- **`memo(Component)`** skips re-rendering a component when its props are shallowly equal (`Object.is` per prop) to last time.
- **`useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b])`** caches a computed value between renders until a dependency changes.
- **`useCallback(fn, [deps])`** caches a function identity; it's `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

They work together. `memo` is defeated if a parent passes a new object or arrow function each render, since `{}` !== `{}`. So you stabilise those props with `useMemo`/`useCallback`. The same applies to values in effect dependencies and context values.

Use them when you've measured a problem: an expensive calculation (filtering thousands of rows), a large subtree that re-renders on every keystroke, or a value that must be stable for an effect. Memoizing everything costs memory and readability, and one unstable prop silently breaks the chain.

Often a structural fix is better: move state down into the component that uses it, or lift expensive content up and pass it as `children` so it isn't re-created when the wrapper's state changes.

The **React Compiler** (stable since v1.0) is a build-time plugin (`babel-plugin-react-compiler`, enabled through the Vite React plugin or Next.js config) that analyses your components and Hooks and inserts fine-grained memoization automatically, including for JSX and callbacks, and even after early returns. With it, most manual `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` becomes unnecessary. It relies on your code following the Rules of React (pure render, no mutation of props/state, Hooks at top level) and skips components it can't prove safe; the `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` rules flag those. Manual memoization remains as an escape hatch for precise control, such as effect dependencies.
takeaways: `memo` skips renders on shallow-equal props; `useMemo` caches values; `useCallback` caches functions
A single new object or function prop defeats `memo`; measure before memoizing
The React Compiler memoizes automatically for code that follows the Rules of React
pitfalls: Wrapping a component in `memo` but passing an inline object or arrow function, so it re-renders anyway.

quiz.q: A memo-wrapped Chart receives options={{ color: 'red' }} written inline in the parent. The parent re-renders. Does Chart re-render?
options: Yes, because a new options object is created each render and fails the shallow comparison
No, memo compares deeply
No, because the values are identical
Only if Chart has state
quiz.explain: memo compares props with Object.is; a fresh object literal is never identical to the previous one.

quiz.q: What does the React Compiler require of your code to optimise it safely?
options: That all components are class components
That components follow the Rules of React, such as pure rendering and no mutation of props or state
That every component is wrapped in memo
That you remove all useState calls
quiz.explain: The compiler's analysis assumes the Rules of React; it bails out on components that break them.

concepts.name: Profiling performance
concepts.summary: Find slow renders with the React DevTools Profiler, the Profiler component and browser performance tools, then fix the real cause.
concepts.why: Performance work without measurement wastes time; the profiler shows exactly which components render, why, and for how long.
concepts.body:
Measure before optimising, and measure a **production build** (`npm run build && npm run preview`): development mode is much slower because of extra checks and Strict Mode double rendering.

The **React DevTools Profiler** (browser extension) records interactions. Start recording, perform the slow action, stop, and inspect each commit:

- The **flame graph** shows which components rendered and how long each took; grey ones didn't render.
- The **ranked** view sorts by self time, pointing at the expensive component.
- Enable "Record why each component rendered" to see whether it was a state change, a parent render, changed props (and which), or a context change.
- "Highlight updates when components render" visually flashes re-rendering components while you use the app.

Typical findings and fixes:

- A keystroke re-renders the whole page because state lives too high: move it down, or pass static parts as `children`.
- A memoized child re-renders because of an unstable prop: stabilise it (or adopt the React Compiler, which DevTools marks with a "Memo" badge).
- A single slow component: memoize the calculation, virtualise a long list (TanStack Virtual, react-window), or move the work off the urgent path with `useTransition`/`useDeferredValue`.

The browser's **Performance** panel complements this; React 19.2 adds custom tracks there showing scheduler priorities and component render timings. For production monitoring, the `<Profiler id onRender>` component reports render durations programmatically (it's disabled in production builds unless you use the profiling build). Also look beyond React: large bundles (split with `lazy`), layout thrashing and slow network waterfalls are frequent culprits.
takeaways: Profile production builds; development mode is deliberately slower
DevTools Profiler shows what rendered, how long, and why
Fix causes: state placement, unstable props, list virtualisation, transitions, code splitting
pitfalls: Optimising based on development-mode timings or console logs instead of a profile.

quiz.q: The Profiler shows a large table re-rendering on every keystroke in an unrelated search box higher up the page. What's the most direct fix?
options: Use a class component for the table
Turn off Strict Mode
Wrap the table in a portal
Move the search state down into a component that doesn't contain the table, or memoize the table
quiz.explain: The table re-renders because it sits under the component whose state changes; isolating the state or memoizing stops the cascade.

concepts.name: Suspense, lazy and use()
concepts.summary: Declare loading states with Suspense boundaries, code-split with lazy, and read promises during render with use().
concepts.why: Suspense replaces scattered isLoading flags with declarative loading UI and is the foundation of streaming and data loading in React 19.
concepts.body:
**Suspense** lets a component "wait" for something before rendering, while you declare the loading UI once, higher up:

```jsx
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <Comments />
</Suspense>
```

If anything inside **suspends**, React shows the nearest boundary's `fallback` until it's ready, then reveals the content. Things that suspend:

- **`lazy`** components: `const Editor = lazy(() => import("./Editor.jsx"))` loads code on first render, which is how you split big bundles by route or feature.
- **`use(promise)`** in React 19: reads the value of a promise during render. If it's pending, the component suspends; if it rejects, the nearest error boundary catches it.
- Suspense-enabled data sources: framework data loading, Server Components, TanStack Query's `useSuspenseQuery`.

`use` is special among Hooks: it can be called conditionally and in loops. The promise must be **stable**: created outside rendering (by a cache, a router loader or a parent) or passed from a Server Component. A promise created in the same component's render is new every time and would suspend forever. Suspense does **not** detect data fetched in an effect.

Design notes:

- Place boundaries where a loading state makes sense to the user. Nested boundaries reveal content progressively, outer first.
- Siblings inside one boundary are revealed together, avoiding a pop-in cascade.
- When an update would hide already-visible content behind a fallback, wrap it in a **transition** (next lesson) and React keeps showing the old UI instead.
- Since React 19, when a component suspends, React shows the fallback immediately and then "pre-warms" siblings, so commits aren't delayed by sibling rendering.
takeaways: Suspense shows the nearest boundary's fallback while children are not ready
`lazy(() => import(...))` code-splits components; `use(promise)` reads promises during render
Promises passed to `use` must be stable (cached or created outside render)
pitfalls: Calling `use(fetch(url))` directly in render, creating a new promise every render.
Expecting Suspense to show a fallback for data fetched in a useEffect.

quiz.q: Which of these will make a Suspense boundary show its fallback?
options: A child rendering a lazy() component whose code hasn't loaded yet
A child that fetches data in useEffect and sets isLoading
A child that throws a regular Error
A child with a slow for-loop in render
quiz.explain: lazy components and use() on pending promises suspend; effects, errors and slow code do not trigger Suspense.

concepts.name: Transitions and useDeferredValue
concepts.summary: Mark updates as non-urgent with useTransition and startTransition, and defer slow parts of the UI with useDeferredValue.
concepts.why: Transitions keep typing and clicking responsive during heavy renders and stop already-visible content flashing back to spinners.
takeaways: `startTransition(() => setX(...))` marks updates as interruptible, low priority
Transitions keep old UI visible instead of falling back to Suspense spinners
`useDeferredValue` gives a lagging copy of a value; pair it with a memoized slow child
pitfalls: Wrapping a controlled input's own state update in a transition, which makes typing lag.

quiz.q: A tab switch suspends while loading. Without a transition the whole panel shows a spinner. What does wrapping setTab in startTransition change?
options: The data loads faster
The Suspense fallback is shown sooner
React keeps showing the current tab until the new one is ready, with isPending true meanwhile
The update is applied synchronously
quiz.explain: Transitions avoid hiding already-revealed content; React waits in the background and keeps the old UI interactive.

concepts.name: Error boundaries
concepts.summary: Catch rendering errors in a subtree and show fallback UI with an error boundary, and report errors from the root.
concepts.why: Without error boundaries, one throwing component unmounts the entire app and leaves users with a blank page.
concepts.body:
If a component throws during rendering, React can't produce a consistent UI, so by default it **unmounts the whole tree**. An **error boundary** limits the damage: it catches errors thrown while rendering its descendants (including in their lifecycle and effects, and rejected promises read with `use`) and renders a fallback instead. Error boundaries are still written as **class components**, the one place modern code needs them. A class becomes a boundary by defining `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` (returns state to render the fallback) and optionally `componentDidCatch(error, info)` (for logging; `info.componentStack` shows where). Most teams use the small **`react-error-boundary`** package instead of writing one: ```jsx Something went wrong.

}> ``` Error boundaries do **not** catch errors in event handlers (those don't happen during rendering; use try/catch and set state), in async code outside rendering (`setTimeout`, a fetch in a handler), or in the boundary itself. Placement is a design choice, like Suspense boundaries: one at the top as a last resort, plus finer ones around independent widgets (a sidebar, a chart, a route) so a failure in one doesn't take down the rest. Offer a retry: `react-error-boundary` gives the fallback a `resetErrorBoundary` function, and changing the boundary's `key` also remounts it fresh. React 19 improves reporting: errors are logged once rather than re-thrown and duplicated, and `createRoot` accepts `onCaughtError` (errors caught by a boundary), `onUncaughtError` and `onRecoverableError` options, which is the right hook for sending errors to a monitoring service.
takeaways: Error boundaries catch render-time errors in their subtree and show a fallback
They're class components (`getDerivedStateFromError`); `react-error-boundary` wraps this nicely
They don't catch event-handler or unrelated async errors; use try/catch there
pitfalls: Expecting an error boundary to catch an exception thrown inside an onClick handler.

quiz.q: A button's onClick throws an error. The button is inside an error boundary. What happens?
options: The boundary shows its fallback
The whole app unmounts
React retries the click
The error propagates as a normal JavaScript error; the boundary doesn't catch it
quiz.explain: Event handlers run outside rendering, so error boundaries don't see their errors; handle them with try/catch.

concepts.name: Actions and form hooks
concepts.summary: Handle async mutations with Actions: form action props, useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic.
concepts.why: Actions are React 19's built-in answer to pending states, errors, optimistic updates and form resets that every app hand-rolled before.
takeaways: `<form action={fn}>` calls `fn(formData)` in a transition and resets the form on success
`useActionState` gives `[state, action, isPending]`; the action gets `(prevState, formData)`
`useFormStatus` reads the parent form's pending state; `useOptimistic` shows temporary UI
pitfalls: Calling `useFormStatus` in the same component that renders the `<form>`; it only reports on a parent form.

quiz.q: A form component calls useFormStatus() and renders <form action={save}>. Why is pending always false?
options: useFormStatus only works with Server Functions
useFormStatus reports on a form rendered above the calling component, not one it renders itself
The form needs an onSubmit handler too
pending is only true in production
quiz.explain: useFormStatus reads the nearest parent form's status; move the call into a child such as a SubmitButton.

quiz.q: What does the action passed to useActionState receive as its first argument?
options: The FormData
The submit event
The previous state
The isPending flag
quiz.explain: It is called as action(previousState, formData), so the first argument is the last returned state.

concepts.name: Fiber, lanes and concurrent rendering
concepts.summary: How React's Fiber architecture splits rendering into interruptible units of work, prioritises updates with lanes, and commits atomically.
concepts.why: Concurrent features, Strict Mode's rules and many subtle bugs only make sense once you know how React schedules and discards work.
concepts.body:
Internally, React represents your component tree as a linked tree of **fibers**: one object per component instance or host element, holding its type, key, props, the list of Hooks (its state), pointers to `child`, `sibling` and `return` (parent), and flags describing pending DOM changes. Hooks state lives on the fiber, which is why Hooks are matched by call order.

React keeps two trees: the **current** tree (what's on screen) and a **work-in-progress** tree being built from it (**double buffering**). Rendering walks the work-in-progress tree one fiber at a time: `beginWork` calls the component and reconciles children, `completeWork` prepares host nodes and bubbles flags up. Because work is a loop over fibers rather than recursion on the call stack, React can **pause** between fibers, yield to the browser (the scheduler works in slices of a few milliseconds), and resume, or throw the work-in-progress away.

The **commit phase** is different: it's synchronous and can't be interrupted. React applies DOM mutations, attaches refs, runs `useLayoutEffect` and swaps the trees, so users never see a half-updated UI. Passive effects (`useEffect`) run afterwards.

Updates are assigned **lanes**, priority bits in a bitmask: discrete input (clicks, key presses) gets a sync lane, continuous events (scroll, mousemove) a higher-than-default lane, ordinary updates the default lane, `startTransition` updates transition lanes, and offscreen or idle work the lowest. A render processes a set of lanes; when a higher-priority update arrives during a transition render, React interrupts, handles the urgent lane, and later **restarts** the transition.

Consequences for your code: a render may run many times or never commit, so render must be pure and side effects belong in effects; reading mutable external data during render can produce **tearing** (different parts of one commit seeing different values), which is what `useSyncExternalStore` prevents. Sync updates are not interruptible, which is exactly why transitions exist.
takeaways: Each component instance is a fiber; Hook state lives on it as an ordered list
Render builds a work-in-progress tree in interruptible units; commit is synchronous and atomic
Lanes prioritise updates: input is sync, transitions are interruptible and can restart
pitfalls: Assuming every render is followed by a commit, e.g. counting renders or logging analytics in the component body.

quiz.q: Why must rendering be free of side effects in concurrent React?
options: Because React may start, pause, restart or abandon a render without committing it
Because the commit phase runs side effects twice
Because fibers are immutable
Because effects run before rendering
quiz.explain: Interruptible rendering means a render's result can be discarded; side effects in it would happen for UI that never appears.

quiz.q: Which part of an update can React interrupt to handle a more urgent update?
options: The commit phase
Rendering a transition's work-in-progress tree
Running useLayoutEffect
Applying DOM mutations
quiz.explain: Only the render phase of non-sync lanes is interruptible; commit is always synchronous.

concepts.name: External stores with useSyncExternalStore
concepts.summary: Subscribe to state that lives outside React safely, without tearing, using useSyncExternalStore.
concepts.why: State libraries, browser APIs and shared caches all live outside React; subscribing to them correctly is required for concurrent rendering.
concepts.body:
Some state isn't owned by React: a Redux or Zustand store, `navigator.onLine`, `window.matchMedia`, a WebSocket cache, `localStorage`. The naive approach (copy it into state in an effect and subscribe) causes a render with stale data first, and, worse, **tearing** under concurrent rendering: if the store changes while React is rendering a transition in slices, components rendered before and after the change show different values in the same commit.

**`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot?)`** solves this:

- `subscribe(callback)` registers a listener React calls whenever the store changes, and returns an unsubscribe function.
- `getSnapshot()` returns the current value. React calls it during render and checks it again before committing; if the value changed mid-render, React re-renders synchronously so the whole tree sees one consistent value.
- `getServerSnapshot()` returns the value to use during server rendering and hydration (where browser APIs don't exist); without it, server rendering throws.

Rules that trip people up:

- `getSnapshot` must return the **same value** (by `Object.is`) when the store hasn't changed. Returning a new object or array each call (`{ ...state }`, `items.filter(...)`) causes an infinite loop. Return immutable snapshots and select or derive outside, or cache.
- Define `subscribe` outside the component (or memoize it); a new function each render re-subscribes every time.
- Updates to external stores are always **synchronous**: they can't be marked as transitions, so a store change that suspends shows the fallback rather than keeping old UI.

This is the primitive state libraries build on; Redux's `useSelector` and Zustand's hooks are implemented with it. Wrap it in a custom Hook (`useOnlineStatus`) and components never know where the data lives.
takeaways: `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` reads external state without tearing
`getSnapshot` must return an identical value while the store is unchanged
Keep `subscribe` stable; external store updates can't be transitions
pitfalls: Returning a freshly built object or filtered array from getSnapshot, causing an infinite re-render loop.

quiz.q: Why does getSnapshot = () => store.items.filter(i => i.visible) cause problems?
options: filter is too slow for render
getSnapshot must be async
Arrays can't be stored in external stores
It returns a new array on every call, so React thinks the store always changed and re-renders endlessly
quiz.explain: React compares snapshots with Object.is; a new array each time never matches, triggering infinite updates.

quiz.q: What problem does useSyncExternalStore prevent that subscribing in useEffect does not?
options: Tearing: different components in one commit seeing different store values during concurrent rendering
Memory leaks from forgotten unsubscribe calls
Slow network requests
Hydration of class components
quiz.explain: React re-checks the snapshot before commit and forces a consistent synchronous render if it changed.

concepts.name: Server Components
concepts.summary: Render components on the server or at build time with React Server Components, and mark interactive parts with 'use client'.
concepts.why: Server Components change where code runs: less JavaScript shipped, direct data access, and a new boundary every modern React developer must understand.
concepts.body:
**React Server Components (RSC)** are components that run only on the server (per request) or at build time. Their code is never sent to the browser. They can be `async` and read data directly:

```jsx
export default async function Note({ id }) {
  const note = await db.notes.get(id);      // no API layer, no effect
  return <article>{note.body}</article>;
}
```

The output is serialised as an RSC payload and merged into the client's tree. Using them requires a bundler and framework integration; in practice that means a framework like Next.js App Router or React Router's RSC support. In such apps, components are Server Components **by default**.

Server Components can't use state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs. For interactivity you add **Client Components**: a module beginning with the `"use client"` directive marks a **boundary**; that module and everything it imports is bundled for the client (and still pre-rendered to HTML by SSR). Composition rules:

- A Server Component can render Client Components and pass them **props that are serialisable**: primitives, plain objects and arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, promises, JSX, and Server Functions. Not class instances or ordinary functions.
- A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one as `children` or another JSX prop, so you can still nest server-rendered content inside client wrappers.
- Push `"use client"` down to the leaves (the button, not the page) to keep bundles small.

Server Components pair with Suspense: wrap a slow async component in `<Suspense>` and the rest streams first. You can also pass an unresolved promise to a Client Component and read it there with `use()`.

Keep secrets server-side with the `server-only` package; any module accidentally imported into a client bundle then fails the build. "Server Components" are not the same as SSR: SSR turns a tree into HTML; RSC decides which components run where.
takeaways: Server Components run on the server/at build, can be async, and ship no JavaScript
`"use client"` marks a boundary; props crossing it must be serialisable
Pass Server Components into Client Components as children; keep client boundaries at the leaves
pitfalls: Adding `"use client"` at the top of a page or layout, turning the whole subtree into client code.
Passing a function or class instance from a Server Component to a Client Component prop.

quiz.q: A Client Component needs to display a Server Component inside it. How is that done?
options: Import the Server Component inside the Client Component file
Add 'use server' to the Client Component
Have a Server Component parent render <ClientWrapper><ServerChild /></ClientWrapper>, passing it as children
It is impossible
quiz.explain: Client modules can't import server components, but they can render server-rendered JSX received as props such as children.

quiz.q: Which prop can a Server Component pass to a Client Component?
options: An onClick arrow function defined in the Server Component
A database connection object
A class instance with methods
A plain object { id: 1, title: 'Hi' }
quiz.explain: Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable; plain objects are fine, ordinary functions and class instances aren't.

concepts.name: Server Functions and server actions
concepts.summary: Call server code from the client with 'use server' functions, use them as form actions, and secure them like public endpoints.
concepts.why: Server Functions replace hand-written API routes for mutations, but each one is a network endpoint with security implications.
concepts.body:
A **Server Function** is an async function marked with `"use server"` that runs on the server but can be called from the client. The framework's bundler replaces it in client code with a reference; calling it sends the arguments over the network, runs the function, and returns the serialised result.

Define them either inline in a Server Component (with `"use server"` at the top of the function body) or in a module that starts with `"use server"`, whose exports all become Server Functions and can be imported by Client Components.

When a Server Function is passed to a form's `action` or called inside a transition, it's commonly called a **server action**. Combined with React 19's form features this is powerful:

```jsx
<form action={createNote}>       // works even before JavaScript has loaded
```

- `useActionState(serverFn, initial)` returns errors and results to the form; with a permalink argument, forms can submit progressively enhanced.
- `useFormStatus` and `useOptimistic` work as with client Actions.
- After a mutation, the framework revalidates or refreshes the affected Server Components (e.g. `revalidatePath` in Next.js).

Security is the main expert concern. Every Server Function is effectively a **public HTTP endpoint**: anyone can call it with any arguments, regardless of whether your UI shows the button. So inside each function:

- **Authenticate and authorise** the caller (check the session, check ownership).
- **Validate** all arguments (e.g. with Zod); `FormData` values are untrusted strings.
- Return only what the client should see; closure variables captured by inline functions are encrypted by frameworks but shouldn't hold secrets.

Server Functions are designed for mutations; calls are processed sequentially, so they're not a good tool for fetching data. Load data in Server Components instead.
takeaways: `"use server"` makes an async function callable from the client over the network
Pass Server Functions to `<form action>` or `useActionState` for progressive enhancement
Treat each one as a public endpoint: authenticate, authorise and validate every call
pitfalls: Relying on the UI hiding a button for security; anyone can invoke the Server Function directly.

quiz.q: A Server Function deleteNote(id) is only rendered for admins in the UI. Is it secure?
options: Yes, because the button is hidden for other users
No; any client can call it with any id, so it must check authorisation itself
Yes, because Server Functions can only be called from Server Components
No, because Server Functions run in the browser
quiz.explain: Server Functions are reachable network endpoints; hiding UI is not access control.

concepts.name: Hydration and streaming SSR
concepts.summary: Render to HTML on the server, stream it with Suspense, and hydrate it on the client without mismatches.
concepts.why: SSR gives fast first paint and SEO; streaming and selective hydration make it fast, and hydration mismatches are a classic production bug.
concepts.body:
**Server-side rendering (SSR)** runs your components on the server to produce HTML, so users see content before JavaScript loads. The client then **hydrates**: React renders the same tree in the browser and attaches event handlers and state to the existing DOM instead of recreating it. ```jsx // client entry hydrateRoot(document.getElementById("root"), ); ``` React's streaming APIs are `renderToPipeableStream` (Node.js streams) and `renderToReadableStream` (Web Streams, for Deno, Bun, edge runtimes). With **streaming**, React sends the HTML shell immediately and leaves **Suspense** fallbacks where content isn't ready. As each boundary resolves on the server, React streams its HTML plus a tiny inline script that swaps it into place, without waiting for the slowest query. Callbacks like `onShellReady` and `onShellError` let you set the status code and handle failures; `onAllReady` waits for everything (useful for crawlers or static generation). For static generation there are `prerender` APIs in `react-dom/static`. Hydration is also incremental. **Selective hydration** hydrates Suspense boundaries independently, and if the user clicks inside a boundary that isn't hydrated yet, React prioritises hydrating that one first. Hydration requires the client's first render to produce **exactly the same output** as the server. A **hydration mismatch** happens when it doesn't, typically from `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `typeof window` checks, locale-dependent formatting, or invalid HTML nesting (a `
` inside a `

`) that the browser rewrote. React 19 logs a single error with a diff of what differed, then discards the server HTML up to the nearest Suspense boundary and renders that part on the client, losing the benefit of SSR there. Fixes: render client-only values in an effect after hydration, use `useId` for generated ids, and `suppressHydrationWarning` only for unavoidable one-element differences such as timestamps. Frameworks wire all of this up; the concepts still decide where you put Suspense boundaries and why a page flickers.
takeaways: SSR renders HTML on the server; `hydrateRoot` attaches React to it on the client
Streaming sends the shell first and fills Suspense boundaries as data resolves
The first client render must match server HTML; avoid time, randomness and window checks in render
pitfalls: Rendering `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()` directly, so server and client output differ and hydration mismatches.

quiz.q: A component renders typeof window === 'undefined' ? 'Server' : 'Client'. What happens on hydration?
options: It shows 'Client' with no issues
The server throws an error
A hydration mismatch, because the client's first render differs from the server HTML
React skips hydrating this component
quiz.explain: The server rendered 'Server' but the client's first render produces 'Client'; render client-only content after an effect instead.

quiz.q: With streaming SSR, what does the browser receive first when one section is wrapped in Suspense and its data is slow?
options: The page shell with that section's fallback, then the section's HTML streamed later
Nothing until all data is ready
An empty div that the client fills via fetch
Only the JavaScript bundle
quiz.explain: React flushes the shell immediately and streams each Suspense boundary's content when it resolves.
